title: Deciding in Milliseconds: Fraud and Risk Systems

know: The fraud types (stolen cards, card testing, account takeover, friendly fraud, merchant fraud) and how the evidence for each arrives.
Where risk scoring sits in the authorization path at Stripe and at Adyen, and the two decision points before and after the issuer answers.

What Stripe has published about Radar's models (2023 and 2026) and what Adyen has published about its fraud models (tree-based ensembles retrained weekly by default, 2024) and its bot-attack model (2026), and what neither has published.
What a merchant can configure: thresholds, rules, lists, reviews.
believe: A risk score is an estimate of a later dispute, and its threshold is a price the merchant sets between lost sales and fraud losses.
A change to a fraud model or rule cannot be judged on the first two weeks of results.
Card testing is a problem of traffic shape that has to be stopped before authorization.
can_do: Say what a given risk decision can and cannot know at the moment it is made.
Set or challenge a block threshold by comparing the cost of a refused good customer with the cost of a fraud case.
Recognize a card-testing attack from its symptoms and name the controls that stop it.
Explain why a fraud system needs a holdout of payments it lets through.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a merchant that judges a new fraud rule after two weeks, the reader names the two things the judgement cannot yet know.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A fashion retailer adds a rule that blocks every payment its provider scores as elevated risk. Two weeks later its fraud disputes are down and it declares the rule a success. What two things is that conclusion missing?
acceptance_criteria.expected: First, most fraud is not yet reported: cardholders take weeks to dispute (Stripe's 2026 figures: 41% of fraud disputes by day 14, 86% by day 60), so the before-and-after comparison is incomplete. Second, a blocked payment never gets a label, so the retailer has not measured how many good customers the rule refused; that needs a holdout or control group of payments let through.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a description of a card-testing attack on a merchant the chapter does not mention, the reader identifies it, says why a model trained on disputes does not catch it, and names where it must be stopped.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A charity's donation form suddenly receives thousands of €1 donations an hour from constantly changing IP addresses; most are declined by the card issuers. What is happening, why would a fraud model that learns from disputes be slow to see it, and where should it be stopped?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Card testing: criminals checking which stolen or guessed card numbers work. No single attempt carries a fraud label and most never become disputes, so the signal is in the shape of the traffic over minutes, not in any one payment. Declined attempts still cost fees and damage the merchant's standing with issuers and networks, so it must be stopped before the request reaches the issuer: rate limits, CAPTCHA or login in front of the form, and the provider's pre-authorization bot blocking.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Every statement about Stripe's or Adyen's models carries its year, old sources are flagged with their age, and the chapter states what is not public: Adyen's fraud-risk model beyond its family and weekly retraining (2024), both companies' criteria and models for accepting a merchant, and Radar's current retraining interval (daily in a 2019 post).

thesis.question: How does a provider decide, during an authorization, whether a payment is fraud?
thesis.claim: A provider cannot know during an authorization whether a payment is fraud. It estimates, before the issuer sees the payment and inside the payment's time budget, how likely the payment is to be disputed as fraud later, using signals from many merchants, and blocks above a threshold; the facts it learns from arrive weeks afterwards and never arrive for payments it blocked, so each threshold trades refused legitimate customers against fraud losses, and the merchant bears both.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that fraud detection is the provider's job: its model classifies each payment as fraud or not, so a merchant who switches it on is protected and has nothing left to decide.
thesis.so_what: A merchant has to set the threshold from its own margins, judge any rule or model change only after the dispute labels have come in, use the provider's backtests and control group to see what its rules refuse, and put limits in front of any endpoint that can start a payment.
thesis.how_why: Both companies document a decision before the payment goes to the network (Stripe marks a blocked payment 'not_sent_to_network'; Adyen's pre-authorization rules) and a second after the issuer answers. The score predicts a dispute: Adyen's documentation says its risk level 'indicates the likelihood that a transaction will result in a fraudulent dispute'. Stripe's October 2026 engineering post gives the delay: 41% of fraud disputes are reported by day 14, 66% by day 30 and 86% by day 60, and a larger model that looked better at first was rolled back once later labels arrived. Because a blocked payment has no outcome, Adyen documents 'control traffic' and Stripe documents altering the score for a small subset of payments, which the chapter reads, as an inference, as a holdout. Card testing has no per-payment label at all, and its declined attempts still cost the merchant fees and standing with issuers, so it has to be stopped before authorization. A refused legitimate customer is a sale the merchant loses, and for accepted fraud Stripe states that the merchant is 'ultimately responsible for payments you choose to accept'. The public record is uneven: Stripe has described Radar's model lineage (to a neural-network-only model in mid-2022, per its 2023 post) and exposes a 0–99 score; Adyen has described its bot-attack feature pipeline (October 2026) and, for its fraud models, tree-based ensembles retrained weekly by default (August 2024), exposes five risk levels, and lets each rule run before or after authorization. Stripe's 'less than 100 milliseconds' is from 2023; Adyen gives 20 ms median and 100 ms at the 99th percentile per model endpoint (January 2025) and no figure for the whole risk decision.

supporting_claims.claim: The provider's risk decision is an estimate of a later fraud dispute, made before the payment reaches the card network and again after the issuer answers, inside the payment's time budget and from signals gathered across many merchants.

The facts the estimate learns from arrive as disputes over about two months, never arrive for blocked payments and take different forms for different kinds of fraud, so any measurement of a model or rule is provisional and needs a holdout.

A block threshold is a price between legitimate customers refused and fraud accepted, both paid by the merchant, who sets it through thresholds, rules, lists and reviews and can test it with the providers' backtests, partial rollouts and control groups.
Card testing has no per-payment label and its declined attempts still cost the merchant, so it is a problem of traffic shape that has to be stopped before authorization.

Stripe and Adyen document the same decision points and kinds of control, and a holdout that Adyen states and Stripe's documentation only implies, but have published very different amounts about their models: Stripe its model lineage and label delay, Adyen its bot-attack pipeline and the family and weekly retraining of its fraud models (2024), and neither its timeout behavior or its merchant underwriting criteria.

The same estimate-now, facts-later structure applies to the merchant being paid: a provider that pays out before the dispute window closes is exposed to each account and scores it or holds funds against that exposure.

role.contribution: Shows the third relocation: the allow-or-block decision moves to the provider's model while the loss stays with the merchant, and supplies the fraud rate and risk score that authentication exemptions depend on.

additional_patterns.applies_to: kinds, where-it-sits, learning, threshold: each supplies the terms the next one uses (dispute and false positive, then the decision points and the score, then labels and the holdout, then the threshold and its tests)

flow.rationale: The reader meets an attack that cost money without any fraud being 'detected' before any term is defined, so the vocabulary arrives as the answer to a problem already felt. The kinds of fraud come first because the rest of the chapter turns on how each kind's evidence arrives. The decision points and the score come before the learning section because a label is only meaningful once the reader knows what was decided without it; the threshold comes after learning because the argument that it is a price, and that a change cannot be judged early, needs the label delay and the holdout. Card testing follows the threshold as the contrast case: the one kind of fraud to which the score, the labels and the threshold do not apply, which is also the answer to the opening scene. Merchant risk is placed after it because it changes the subject from the payer to the payee and must not interrupt the argument about payments, and before the comparison so that the gap in underwriting can be listed with the other gaps. Larkfield's worked case needs every mechanism, so it follows the comparison; the failures close the body. Putting card testing first, where the scene suggests it, would explain the exception before the rule it is an exception to.

hook.content: At 03:14 on a Saturday a €1 payment arrives at a studio's booking page. The card number is real, the expiry date is right and the three-digit code matches. Nothing was stolen from the studio, its platform or its payment provider; the number was taken somewhere else, months ago. The only person who knows this payment is fraud is the cardholder, who is asleep and will find out from a bank statement some weeks from now.

bridge.from_reader_world: An engineer expects a fraud check to be a classifier: a request goes in, 'fraud' or 'not fraud' comes out, and the provider that runs it owns the answer.
bridge.to_topic: No such answer exists when the payment is made. What exists is a prediction of a dispute that may be filed weeks later, a threshold somebody chose, and a bill for both kinds of error that goes to the merchant.

thesis_statement.text: A provider cannot know during an authorization whether a payment is fraud; it estimates the chance of a later fraud dispute before the issuer sees the payment, blocks above a threshold, and learns weeks later and never about what it blocked, so each threshold trades refused customers against fraud losses and the merchant bears both.

evidence.what: "A payment is considered fraudulent when the cardholder didn't authorize it. Most fraudulent payments are made using stolen cards or card numbers."
evidence.shows: Fraud is defined by a fact about the cardholder's consent that nobody in the payment path can observe when the payment is made.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A provider therefore does not detect fraud during an authorization: it estimates how likely the payment is to be disputed as fraud later, blocks above a threshold before the issuer is asked, and learns weeks afterwards and only about what it let through, so the threshold is a price whose two costs both fall on the merchant.

sections.heading: Setting the Scene at Larkfield: The Card-Testing Weekend
sections.controlling_idea: Over one weekend 61,000 stolen card numbers were tested through one studio's booking widget; Larkfield lost no data and almost no payment was ever disputed, yet it paid €4,100 and the studio could not take payments for 31 hours.

advances_thesis.how: Poses the chapter's hardest case first: an attack in which no single payment looks like fraud and no dispute label ever arrives.

flow.rationale: The attack, then what it cost and what it did not involve, then the questions it left; the questions are the chapter's sections, so they come last.

transition_in.carries_over: The introduction's claim that a provider estimates and a merchant pays.
transition_in.introduces: One weekend at Larkfield in which the estimate had nothing to work with.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: On the weekend of 8–9 August 2026 bots sent 61,000 one-euro drop-in payments, each with a different stolen card number, through the public booking widget of one studio.

evidence.what: The Card-Testing Weekend, 8–9 August 2026: 61,000 stolen card numbers, €1 drop-in payments, one studio's public booking widget (ledger). Illustrative split, labeled as assumption: about 38,400 attempts blocked by the provider before the network, 19,700 declined by issuers, 2,900 approved.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The weekend cost Larkfield €4,100 in fees and refunds and cost the studio 31 hours without online payments, although Larkfield stored no card numbers and the approved payments were refunded before they could become disputes.

Illustrative split, labeled as assumption: €2,900 refunded on the approved €1 payments and about €1,200 in provider fees on attempts and refunds; each unrefunded payment could have become a dispute with an illustrative €15.00 fee.

sections.heading: Five Kinds of Fraud, and How the Evidence for Each Arrives
sections.controlling_idea: Payment fraud is five different problems, and what separates them for a system builder is when and in what form the evidence that a payment was fraud arrives.

advances_thesis.how: Supplies the vocabulary (dispute, fraud label, false positive) and shows that only one of the five kinds produces the per-payment label a model can learn from directly.

flow.rationale: The definition and the size of the problem come first, then the five kinds side by side, then what the table implies for anyone building a detector. The two consequences of the table are separate units: first the several prediction problems, then, from rarity, the false positive.

transition_in.carries_over: Femke's second question: why a system built to catch fraud stopped only part of an attack made entirely of stolen cards.
transition_in.introduces: What 'fraud' covers, and how each kind becomes known.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Card fraud becomes known to the payment system only as a dispute filed by the cardholder's bank, the loss from it falls on the merchant, and it is concentrated in online payments.

evidence.what: "the business suffers a loss equal to the amount of the payment, and the cost of any goods or services already provided. The business is also subject to a dispute fee."
evidence.shows: The default bearer of a fraud dispute is the merchant, not the provider or the issuer.
evidence.source: Stripe documentation, 'Types of fraud', https://docs.stripe.com/disputes/prevention/fraud-types (n.d., accessed November 2026)

evidence.what: EEA, 2024: the card fraud rate by value was 0.091% for remote payments against 0.007% for non-remote payments, "13 times higher in value".
evidence.shows: Fraud is rare in absolute terms and an online problem, which is why the scoring this chapter describes is aimed at online card payments.
evidence.source: EBA and ECB, '2025 Report on payment fraud' (EBA/REP/2025/40), https://www.ecb.europa.eu/press/intro/publications/pdf/ecb.ebaecb202512.en.pdf (December 2025)

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The five kinds (stolen-card fraud, card testing, account takeover, friendly fraud and merchant fraud) differ in who is deceived and in how the evidence arrives: as a dispute weeks later, as no per-payment evidence at all, or as a property of an account.

evidence.what: Table: kind | what happens | how the evidence arrives | who carries the loss by default. Stolen card: dispute weeks later; merchant. Card testing ("testing a card (or multiple cards) on one site to see if it's still valid before using it on another site"): no per-payment evidence; merchant pays fees, a later victim merchant takes the fraud. Account takeover (absent from both companies' risk-product documentation; the row follows Adyen's payment-fraud guide of 8 December 2025: "when fraudsters get access to shoppers’ accounts"): dispute or customer complaint; merchant. Friendly fraud ("a legitimate cardholder makes a purchase, but then disputes it at a later date"): the same dispute signal as real fraud; merchant unless it wins the dispute. Merchant fraud ("a fraudulent business takes payments without providing the services or goods"): many disputes against one account; the platform or provider if funds cannot be recovered.
evidence.shows: Only the first kind yields the clean, late, per-payment label; the others need different detectors.
evidence.source: Stripe documentation, 'Types of fraud', https://docs.stripe.com/disputes/prevention/fraud-types (n.d., accessed November 2026)

transition_in.carries_over: Fraud as an unauthorized payment that surfaces as a dispute.
transition_in.introduces: The five kinds and the form their evidence takes.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Because only stolen-card fraud yields clean per-payment evidence, a single verdict on a payment hides at least three prediction problems, one for each form the evidence takes: a dispute weeks later, no per-payment evidence (card testing), and a property of an account (merchant fraud).

evidence.what: The table's rows mapped to the three forms of evidence: dispute weeks later (stolen cards, account takeover, friendly fraud), none per payment (card testing), a property of an account (merchant fraud). The author's reading, labeled as such.
evidence.shows: Why one score per payment answers several different questions.

transition_in.carries_over: Five kinds whose evidence arrives in three different forms.
transition_in.introduces: The first consequence for a single score: several prediction problems.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Because fraud is rare, the most frequent error of a fraud detector is a false positive, a legitimate payment refused: at the EBA/ECB remote rate by number, a detector wrong about 1% of legitimate payments refuses some fifteen good payments for every fraudulent one it could catch.

evidence.what: EBA/ECB report for 2024: remote card fraud rate by number of payments 0.068%, about 7 payments in every 10,000; a detector wrong about 1% of legitimate payments refuses about 100 good payments in those 10,000, some fifteen for every fraudulent one it could catch. The author's arithmetic, labeled as such.
evidence.shows: Sets up the cost of false positives before any mechanism is described.
evidence.source: European Banking Authority and European Central Bank, '2025 Report on payment fraud' (EBA/REP/2025/40), https://www.ecb.europa.eu/press/intro/publications/pdf/ecb.ebaecb202512.en.pdf (December 2025)

transition_in.carries_over: The first consequence: one verdict, several prediction problems.
transition_in.introduces: The second consequence, from rarity: the false positive.

sections.heading: Where the Decision Sits: Before the Issuer, and Again After
sections.controlling_idea: Both providers make a first risk decision before the payment is sent to the card network and a second after the issuer answers, and the score behind both is an estimate of a later fraud dispute computed inside the payment's time budget from signals collected across many merchants.

advances_thesis.how: Establishes the mechanism the thesis describes: an estimate, in front of the issuer, on a time budget, from cross-merchant signals.

flow.rationale: The order of the payment itself: the decision before the network, the decision after the issuer's answer, then what the number in both means, how long it may take, and what it is computed from. The score is defined after the two decision points because the reader needs to know what is being decided before learning what the number estimates.

transition_in.carries_over: Fraud that cannot be known at payment time and a score that will often be wrong about good payments.
transition_in.introduces: Where in the authorization path that score is used.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The first decision is made before the card network and the issuer see the payment, so a blocked payment is one the bank was never asked about.

evidence.what: Stripe: the outcome of a payment blocked for risk shows `"network_status": "not_sent_to_network"`, `"type": "blocked"`, `"reason": "highest_risk_level"`.
evidence.shows: Stripe's own record says the block happened before the network.
evidence.source: Stripe documentation, 'Risk evaluation', https://docs.stripe.com/radar/risk-evaluation (n.d., accessed November 2026)

evidence.what: Adyen: "Pre-authorization: the risk rule conditions are assessed before the payment is authorized. This saves issuer and scheme fees compared to blocking after authorization."
evidence.shows: Adyen documents the same placement and gives the economic reason for it.
evidence.source: Adyen documentation, 'Configure your risk profile', https://docs.adyen.com/risk-management/configure-your-risk-profile (n.d., accessed November 2026)

evidence.what: Figure: the authorization path with two decision points, one before the network and one after the issuer's answer.
evidence.shows: Shows the two points and which signals exist at each.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A second decision is made after the issuer answers, because some signals (the result of the security-code and address checks, the outcome of authentication) exist only then, and review by a person comes later still, after the money is already reserved.

evidence.what: Adyen: in post-authorization rules "the risk evaluation can take extra signals into account that are only available after authorization. For example authentication results, CVC/CVV codes, or AVS responses."
evidence.shows: Names the signals that do not exist at the first decision point.
evidence.source: Adyen documentation, 'Configure your risk profile', https://docs.adyen.com/risk-management/configure-your-risk-profile (n.d., accessed November 2026)

evidence.what: Stripe: built-in rules "block certain payments that the card issuer approved"; "Payments placed into review are typically already successfully processed, unless you capture authorized payments later." Adyen: with capture delay for case management, "up to seven calendar days to reject a transaction".
evidence.shows: Both companies document blocking after approval and a human review that happens after authorization.
evidence.source: Stripe documentation, 'Rules', https://docs.stripe.com/radar/rules (n.d., accessed November 2026); Stripe documentation, 'Reviews', https://docs.stripe.com/radar/reviews (n.d., accessed November 2026); Adyen documentation, 'Case management', https://docs.adyen.com/risk-management/case-management (n.d., accessed November 2026)

transition_in.carries_over: The decision in front of the issuer.
transition_in.introduces: The decision after the issuer's answer and the review queue behind it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The risk score used at both points is an estimate of how likely the payment is to end in a fraud dispute, exposed by Stripe's product, Radar, as a number from 0 to 99 with the levels normal, elevated and highest, and by Adyen's, Protect, as one of five levels. In the rest of the chapter 'the score' means the estimate, on any scale.

evidence.what: Adyen: the risk level "indicates the likelihood that a transaction will result in a fraudulent dispute", "ranging from Very Low to Very High"; "By default, the block threshold for this rule is set to high risk and above."
evidence.shows: The score is defined against a future event, the dispute, not against a present fact.
evidence.source: Adyen documentation, 'Machine learning rules', https://docs.adyen.com/risk-management/configure-your-risk-profile/machine-learning-rules (n.d., accessed November 2026)

evidence.what: Stripe: "a risk score that ranges from 0–99"; "By default, a score of 65 or above indicates elevated risk, while a score of 75 or above indicates high risk"; high-risk payments are blocked by default and elevated-risk payments allowed. The score is returned only on certain Radar plans (the plans are named Lite, Standard, Plus and Pro as of November 2026).
evidence.shows: Stripe exposes a finer scale with two published cut-offs; neither documents how a score or level maps to a percentage (Stripe's risk-settings page calls its classic risk score "the probability that a payment results in a fraudulent dispute or early fraud warning" and says the block rule built on it is being deprecated).
evidence.source: Stripe documentation, 'Risk evaluation', https://docs.stripe.com/radar/risk-evaluation (n.d., accessed November 2026); Stripe documentation, 'How Radar works' (plans), https://docs.stripe.com/radar/how-radar-works (n.d., accessed November 2026)

transition_in.carries_over: Two decision points that both use a score.
transition_in.introduces: What the score is an estimate of, and how each company exposes it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The estimate has to fit inside the payment's time budget, for which Stripe published 'less than 100 milliseconds' in 2023 and Adyen has published nothing, and only Stripe documents what happens when the evaluation fails. Traffic allocation (a rule applied to only a share of payments) is glossed here because the requirements table uses it before the threshold section explains it.

evidence.what: Stripe, 2023: Radar "makes this decision, accurately, in less than 100 milliseconds" (evidence age: more than three years); 2024: "the time required to retrieve features directly impacts the overall payment API latency"; 2026: the model "scores payments in milliseconds".
evidence.shows: The risk decision is a synchronous step of the payment call and feature retrieval is part of its budget; the specific figure is old.
evidence.source: Ryan Drapeau, 'How we built it: Stripe Radar', https://stripe.dev/blog/how-we-built-it-stripe-radar (29 March 2023; evidence age: more than three years); Ben Mears, 'Shepherd: How Stripe adapted Chronon to scale ML feature development', https://stripe.dev/blog/shepherd-how-stripe-adapted-chronon-to-scale-ml-feature-development (15 April 2024); Ryan Drapeau and Sai Samant, 'Scaling Radar: Fighting fraud with agent-assisted machine learning', https://stripe.dev/blog/scaling-radar-fighting-fraud-with-agent-assisted-machine-learning (19 October 2026)

evidence.what: Stripe: "an error might cause risk evaluation to fail. If this happens, Stripe reports the payment as having unknown risk"; the documented example outcome shows the payment authorized with `risk_level` `unknown`.
evidence.shows: The one documented failure behavior is to let the payment proceed.
evidence.source: Stripe documentation, 'Risk evaluation', https://docs.stripe.com/radar/risk-evaluation (n.d., accessed November 2026)

evidence.what: Requirements table: how fast (Stripe: under 100 ms, 2023; Adyen: no figure for the whole decision; its January 2025 engineering post gives the model-serving service "a p50 of 20 ms and p99 of 100 ms" per request and "between 2 and 5" model endpoints per transaction), how consistent (the same answer for a retry: Stripe pins retries to the same traffic-allocation bucket), how available (documented for neither), what happens on failure (Stripe: unknown risk, payment proceeds; Adyen: not documented). Followed by an INFERENCE, NOT DOCUMENTED block on timeouts.
evidence.shows: Collects what is public about the non-functional side of the decision and marks the gaps.

transition_in.carries_over: A score defined as an estimate.
transition_in.introduces: The time it has and what happens when it cannot be computed.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The inputs to the estimate, called fraud signals, come mostly from the provider's view across many merchants and from data its client-side script collects, so how a merchant integrates decides how much the model can see.

evidence.what: Stripe, 2026: "a credit card that is new and untrusted to one business might have years of history elsewhere on Stripe that proves it's OK or an IP address may link activity across several cards and accounts."
evidence.shows: The network effect in one sentence: one merchant's unknown card is known to the provider.
evidence.source: Ryan Drapeau and Sai Samant, 'Scaling Radar: Fighting fraud with agent-assisted machine learning', https://stripe.dev/blog/scaling-radar-fighting-fraud-with-agent-assisted-machine-learning (19 October 2026)

evidence.what: Adyen: models "can detect recent fraud on a shopper's email address or recognize a good shopper because of a recent in-person payment on a card on the Adyen platform"; "Adyen collects data about how shoppers interact with and use the payment form."
evidence.shows: Adyen documents a cross-channel signal and client-side collection.
evidence.source: Adyen documentation, 'Risk management', https://docs.adyen.com/risk-management (n.d., accessed November 2026); Adyen documentation, 'Fraud data collection', https://docs.adyen.com/risk-management/fraud-data-collection (n.d., accessed November 2026)

evidence.what: Stripe's card-testing guidance lists the data a merchant can send to its card-testing models and marks "Advanced fraud detection" (device and activity signals collected by its JavaScript library) as "Highest impact".
evidence.shows: The way card data is collected (chapter 22) decides which signals exist.
evidence.source: Stripe documentation, 'Card testing', https://docs.stripe.com/disputes/prevention/card-testing (n.d., accessed November 2026)

transition_in.carries_over: An estimate that must be fast.
transition_in.introduces: What it is computed from, and the term fraud signal.

sections.heading: Learning Weeks Later: Labels, Delay and the Payments Nobody Sees
sections.controlling_idea: A fraud model learns from disputes that arrive over about two months and never arrive for payments it blocked, so its measured performance is always provisional and it must let some risky payments through to keep learning.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the dated evidence for the second half of the thesis (the facts arrive weeks afterwards and never for blocked payments) and records what each company has published about the model that does the learning.

flow.rationale: The delay comes first because the rollback is its consequence; the missing labels for blocked payments are a second, separate gap, answered by the holdout; the feedback loop names what the two gaps have in common; the published model detail closes the section because it is the system the earlier paragraphs describe.

transition_in.carries_over: A score that estimates a future dispute.
transition_in.introduces: How and when the system finds out whether the estimate was right.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The fact a model learns from, called a label, is the fraud dispute, and Stripe's 2026 figures show it arriving slowly: 41% of fraud disputes by day 14, 66% by day 30 and 86% by day 60.

evidence.what: "For a payment made with a stolen card, it could take weeks for the cardholder to notice and report it to their bank. When Stripe receives the fraudulent dispute, we gain a fraud label for a payment we scored weeks earlier." Chart: the cumulative share of fraudulent disputes reported reaches "41% by day 14, 66% by day 30, and 86% by day 60 after the payment".
evidence.shows: Quantifies the delay: after two weeks fewer than half of the eventual labels exist.
evidence.source: Ryan Drapeau and Sai Samant, 'Scaling Radar: Fighting fraud with agent-assisted machine learning', https://stripe.dev/blog/scaling-radar-fighting-fraud-with-agent-assisted-machine-learning (19 October 2026)

evidence.what: Figure: the label-arrival curve with the points 41%, 66% and 86% at days 14, 30 and 60.
evidence.shows: Makes the share of labels missing at any review date visible.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Because of that delay a model or rule that looks better after two weeks can turn out worse, which is what Stripe reports happened to a larger Radar model it had to roll back.

evidence.what: A larger model "looked better in offline tests and in early results of a production experiment. But, as more fraud reports arrived, its measured performance fell below the earlier model's, and we had to roll back"; training without downsampling had added "more fraudulent examples labeled as legitimate, about 20 times more".
evidence.shows: The provider with the most data misjudged a change on early labels; a merchant judging a rule after two weeks has less to go on.
evidence.source: Ryan Drapeau and Sai Samant, 'Scaling Radar: Fighting fraud with agent-assisted machine learning', https://stripe.dev/blog/scaling-radar-fighting-fraud-with-agent-assisted-machine-learning (19 October 2026)

transition_in.carries_over: Labels that take two months to arrive.
transition_in.introduces: What happens to a judgement made before they have.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A blocked payment never receives a label at all, so a provider needs a holdout: Adyen documents one (control traffic) and Stripe documents a device that reads as one.

evidence.what: Stripe: "For a small subset of payments, Stripe modifies the reported risk score so we can measure the performance of our models and obtain data for subsequent model development."
evidence.shows: Stripe documents that it modifies the reported score for a small subset to measure its models; that this is a holdout is the author's inference.
evidence.source: Stripe documentation, 'Risk evaluation', https://docs.stripe.com/radar/risk-evaluation (n.d., accessed November 2026)

evidence.what: Adyen: "A very small percentage of all transactions is randomly selected to be part of control traffic. Control traffic transactions are settled regardless of their risk evaluation." Excluded: "Transactions with an amount of EUR 2000 or higher".
evidence.shows: Adyen documents the same device and bounds its cost.
evidence.source: Adyen documentation, 'Control traffic', https://docs.adyen.com/risk-management/control-traffic (n.d., accessed November 2026)

transition_in.carries_over: Labels that arrive late.
transition_in.introduces: Labels that never arrive, and the holdout that replaces them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Together these make a feedback loop: the system's own decisions determine which outcomes it will later see, and merchants add to the loop when they report a payment as fraudulent.

evidence.what: Stripe: refunding a payment with the reason `fraudulent` adds the card fingerprint and email address to the default block lists, and "Our AI models respond to feedback you share with us".
evidence.shows: The merchant is a second, faster source of labels.
evidence.source: Stripe documentation, 'Risk evaluation', https://docs.stripe.com/radar/risk-evaluation (n.d., accessed November 2026)

evidence.what: Friendly fraud arrives through the same dispute signal as stolen-card fraud, so the labels are noisy in both directions. The author's judgement, labeled as such.
evidence.shows: Qualifies the label as evidence.

transition_in.carries_over: Late labels and missing labels.
transition_in.introduces: The term feedback loop and the merchant's part in it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Stripe has published the lineage and size of the model that does this learning, Adyen's documentation says little about its fraud-risk model beyond a 2024 post's model family and weekly retraining, and Stripe has not said how often Radar is retrained now.

evidence.what: Stripe, 2023 (evidence age: more than three years): from "relatively simple ML models (e.g., logistic regression)" to an ensemble of XGBoost and a deep neural network, then "in mid-2022 ... to a pure DNN-only model". Stripe, 2026: the transaction-fraud model is named Shield and was trained on "roughly 800 million" sampled transactions; a version trained on more data "grew to roughly 30 million parameters, three times its previous size" and was rolled back (the size of the production model is not stated); a new training configuration "improved recall by over 8%" in a controlled comparison; "regular retraining" with no interval stated; a Stripe engineering post of 7 May 2019 said Radar's models were trained and deployed "on a daily cadence" (evidence age: 7 years). Adyen, 16 August 2024 (evidence age: 2 years): fraud models "currently based on tree-based ensembling models", retrained "on a default weekly cadence".
evidence.shows: The public record on Stripe's model, with dates; the 2026 post confirms the 2023 architecture and adds scale.
evidence.source: Ryan Drapeau, 'How we built it: Stripe Radar', https://stripe.dev/blog/how-we-built-it-stripe-radar (29 March 2023; evidence age: more than three years); Ryan Drapeau and Sai Samant, 'Scaling Radar: Fighting fraud with agent-assisted machine learning', https://stripe.dev/blog/scaling-radar-fighting-fraud-with-agent-assisted-machine-learning (19 October 2026)

evidence.what: Adyen's documentation says only that the premium tier offers "Machine learning powered fraud detection using global transaction data".
evidence.shows: Nothing comparable is public for Adyen's fraud-risk model.
evidence.source: Adyen documentation, 'Risk management', https://docs.adyen.com/risk-management (n.d., accessed November 2026)

transition_in.carries_over: The feedback loop as a mechanism.
transition_in.introduces: What each company has published about the model inside it.

sections.heading: The Threshold Is a Price: Refused Customers against Fraud Losses
sections.controlling_idea: The block threshold trades legitimate customers refused against fraud accepted, both costs fall on the merchant, and the merchant's real configuration choices (threshold, rules, lists, review) are ways of setting that price and testing it.

advances_thesis.how: Argues the thesis's final clause and gives the reader the rule for setting or challenging a threshold.

flow.rationale: The trade and who pays come first; the break-even rule turns it into a number; the four configurations are the ways to act on the number; rules get their own paragraph because they are the configuration that most often goes wrong; testing closes the section because every earlier choice has to be checked against the label delay of the previous section.

transition_in.carries_over: A model whose errors are only visible weeks later and partly never.
transition_in.introduces: Who chooses how strict it is, and on what basis.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Because a model is proven right only weeks later and never for blocked payments, someone has to choose how strict it is; wherever the threshold is set it trades two errors, fraud allowed and good customers refused, and the merchant pays for both.

evidence.what: Stripe: "you're ultimately responsible for payments you choose to accept, including those that are later disputed or found to be fraudulent."
evidence.shows: The provider makes the estimate and the merchant keeps the loss.
evidence.source: Stripe documentation, 'Risk evaluation', https://docs.stripe.com/radar/risk-evaluation (n.d., accessed November 2026)

evidence.what: Stripe, 2023 (evidence age: more than three years): "Radar incorrectly blocks just 0.1%" of legitimate payments. A vendor's network-wide average, not any one merchant's rate.
evidence.shows: Even the vendor's own figure concedes the second error exists; it does not tell a merchant its own false-positive rate.
evidence.source: Ryan Drapeau, 'How we built it: Stripe Radar', https://stripe.dev/blog/how-we-built-it-stripe-radar (29 March 2023; evidence age: more than three years)

evidence.what: Figure: a threshold slider between two piles, refused good customers and accepted fraud.
evidence.shows: Fixes the trade as one dial with two costs.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The threshold that minimizes cost blocks a payment only when its chance of fraud times the cost of a fraud case exceeds its chance of being legitimate times the cost of refusing a good customer, so it depends on the merchant's margins and not on the model.

evidence.what: Adyen's guidance: retailers with thin margins should set a Low or Medium threshold because "the cost of a fraud case ... largely outweighs the cost of a false decline"; sellers of digital goods a High or Very High one because "the cost of a false decline (potential loss of lifetime value) mostly outweighs the cost of a fraud case".
evidence.shows: A provider's own documentation frames the threshold as an economic choice by business type.
evidence.source: Adyen documentation, 'Machine learning rules', https://docs.adyen.com/risk-management/configure-your-risk-profile/machine-learning-rules (n.d., accessed November 2026)

evidence.what: Break-even probability = cost of a refused customer ÷ (cost of a refused customer + cost of a fraud case). Illustrative: a €200 item that cost the retailer €160, with a €15 dispute fee: a fraud case loses €175, a refused customer the €40 margin, so 40 ÷ (40 + 175) = 19%. Adyen's documentation states the dependence: "The optimal blocking threshold ... depends on your business model and the difference in cost between a fraud case and a false decline."
evidence.shows: Turns the trade into arithmetic the reader can redo with its own numbers.

transition_in.carries_over: Two errors, both paid by the merchant.
transition_in.introduces: The rule that prices one against the other.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A merchant can run the provider's model in four configurations, each giving more control at more cost: the default, its own threshold, its own rules and lists on top, and manual review of the middle band. On Adyen these live in a risk profile, a named set of risk settings.

evidence.what: Trade-off table: configuration | what you control | what it costs | when it is right. Rows: provider default; own threshold (Stripe risk settings and presets, Adyen risk level per profile); model plus rules and lists; plus manual review (Stripe review queue after processing; Adyen case management with up to seven days).
evidence.shows: The realistic designs side by side; the facts in the cells are cited in this and the previous sections.
evidence.source: Stripe documentation, 'Risk evaluation', https://docs.stripe.com/radar/risk-evaluation (n.d., accessed November 2026); Adyen documentation, 'Machine learning rules', https://docs.adyen.com/risk-management/configure-your-risk-profile/machine-learning-rules (n.d., accessed November 2026); Adyen documentation, 'Case management', https://docs.adyen.com/risk-management/case-management (n.d., accessed November 2026)

transition_in.carries_over: A price that depends on the merchant.
transition_in.introduces: The four ways a merchant can set it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Rules are the merchant's own, explainable additions to the model, whose actions are allow, block and, between the two, review by a person or a request for 3-D Secure (asking the issuer to check who is paying), and their danger is the allow rule, which overrides the model for everything it matches.

evidence.what: Stripe: "Implement any allow rules minimally, because they override the Stripe default rules, along with any other custom rules that match the same criteria"; "You can create a maximum of 200 transaction rules and 100 account rules." Adyen: "Allow rules have the highest priority within a risk profile." Stripe's example of the third action: `Request 3D Secure if :risk_level: != 'normal' and :amount_in_usd: > 25`.
evidence.shows: Both products are a model plus a rules engine in which allow wins; both name 3-D Secure as an action between allow and block.
evidence.source: Stripe documentation, 'Rules', https://docs.stripe.com/radar/rules (n.d., accessed November 2026); Adyen documentation, 'Configure your risk profile', https://docs.adyen.com/risk-management/configure-your-risk-profile (n.d., accessed November 2026)

transition_in.carries_over: The third configuration, model plus rules.
transition_in.introduces: What a rule can do and where it bites back.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Any change to a threshold or rule should be tested before and during rollout with the tools both providers document (a backtest on past payments, a partial or shadow rollout, a live experiment) and judged only once the labels are in, because the backtest and the control group are the only places a merchant can see what a rule refuses.

evidence.what: Stripe: the rule tester "runs a simulation on the last 6 months of charges"; traffic allocation applies a rule to a percentage of matching payments, 0% evaluates it in shadow, and "Radar assigns all attempts for the same transaction to the same allocation bucket, so each retry receives the same outcome as the original attempt." Adyen: custom rules can be backtested (premium), and risk experiments "A/B test two risk profiles against each other" on "real transactions".
evidence.shows: The tools to answer 'what would this rule have refused' exist at both providers.
evidence.source: Stripe documentation, 'Rules', https://docs.stripe.com/radar/rules (n.d., accessed November 2026); Adyen documentation, 'Risk management', https://docs.adyen.com/risk-management (n.d., accessed November 2026); Adyen documentation, 'Run A/B test experiments', https://docs.adyen.com/risk-management/run-ab-test-experiments (n.d., accessed November 2026)

transition_in.carries_over: Rules that can silently override the model or refuse good customers.
transition_in.introduces: How to test a change, and when to judge it.

sections.heading: Card Testing: Fraud That Leaves No Label
sections.controlling_idea: Card testing produces no per-payment label and few disputes, its declined attempts still cost the merchant, and the only place to stop it is before authorization, by limiting the endpoint and by models that watch the shape of traffic.

advances_thesis.how: Argues the one kind of fraud the estimate-and-learn mechanism of the earlier sections cannot handle, and answers the scene's question.

flow.rationale: What the attack is and why it is run, why the dispute-trained model is slow to see it, why waiting for the issuer to decline is not good enough, then the layered controls. The cost of declined attempts has to come before the controls because it is the reason the controls sit in front of authorization.

transition_in.carries_over: A score, a threshold and a feedback loop that all depend on dispute labels.
transition_in.introduces: The kind of fraud that produces none.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Unlike the score, threshold and feedback loop, which run on dispute labels, card testing produces almost none: it is the use of a merchant's checkout to find out which stolen or guessed card numbers work, and it is worth doing because a validated card is used for real fraud elsewhere within days.

evidence.what: Adyen, 2026: "verification, where bots iterate through lists of stolen credentials using low-amount transactions to identify active cards; and enumeration, where scripts systematically guess missing fields, such as CVVs or expiry dates, within specific BIN ranges."
evidence.shows: Two forms of one attack; the merchant is a tool, not the target.
evidence.source: Jaap Stefels, 'Catching card testing at scale with real-time features', https://www.adyen.com/knowledge-hub/catching-card-testing-at-scale (4 October 2026)

evidence.what: Visa, 2024 (its own data): "Thirty three percent of enumerated accounts experienced fraud within five days"; enumeration causes "$1.1B annually in fraud losses".
evidence.shows: Why the attack is run and why networks police it.
evidence.source: Visa press release, 'Visa Announces Generative AI-Powered Fraud Solution to Combat Account Attacks', https://usa.visa.com/about-visa/newsroom/press-releases.releaseId.20661.html (7 May 2024)

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A model trained on disputes is slow to see card testing because each attempt looks ordinary and none carries a label; the evidence is in the shape of traffic over minutes, which is what Adyen's 2026 description of its bot-attack model is built around. Adyen's model judges a payment by the recent traffic of its slice, computed as the traffic streams in, before the issuer is asked.

evidence.what: Adyen, 2026: "Unlike chargeback fraud ... card testing offers no explicit transaction-level signal." "Rotational attacks: Fraudsters continuously rotate details—such as IP addresses—to stay well below baseline velocity thresholds." Features are computed on "subslices" such as a BIN range at one merchant; a feature language is compiled to Apache Spark for training and to Apache Kafka and Flink for live scoring, and "Flink writes these streaming metrics to an Apache Cassandra feature store, where the risk engine fetches the latest subslice values to make real-time block/allow decisions before sending transactions to the issuer."
evidence.shows: The one substantial engineering description Adyen has published about a fraud model: aggregate features, streaming, a decision in front of the issuer.
evidence.source: Jaap Stefels, 'Catching card testing at scale with real-time features', https://www.adyen.com/knowledge-hub/catching-card-testing-at-scale (4 October 2026)

evidence.what: Figure: single payments that each look normal beside the aggregate view of one slice of traffic in which the attack is obvious.
evidence.shows: Shows why the unit of detection is the traffic slice and not the payment.

transition_in.carries_over: An attack made of small, ordinary-looking payments.
transition_in.introduces: Why per-payment scoring misses it and what detects it instead.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Attempts that the issuer declines still cost the merchant: in fees, in its standing with issuers, and in the card networks' monitoring, which counts declined attempts as well as approved ones.

evidence.what: Stripe: "A high decline rate might damage the reputation of your business with card issuers and card networks, which makes all of your transactions appear riskier"; symptoms include "A spike in requests with 402 errors".
evidence.shows: The harm outlasts the attack and reaches the merchant's legitimate payments.
evidence.source: Stripe documentation, 'Card testing', https://docs.stripe.com/disputes/prevention/card-testing (n.d., accessed November 2026)

evidence.what: Visa's Acquirer Monitoring Program (fact sheet, 2025) defines an enumeration ratio as "[Count of Enumerated Authorization Transactions (Approved + Declined)] ÷ [Count of Authorization Transactions (Approved+ Declined)]", with thresholds of 2,000 basis points and 300,000 enumerated transactions in a month, and "requires acquirers to take proactive steps to prevent merchants from exceeding enumeration thresholds".
evidence.shows: The network counts declined attempts, so letting the issuer decline them is not a defense.
evidence.source: Visa, 'Visa Acquirer Monitoring Program Overview' fact sheet, https://corporate.visa.com/content/dam/VCOM/corporate/visa-perspectives/security-and-trust/documents/visa-acquirer-monitoring-program-fact-sheet-2025.pdf (2025)

transition_in.carries_over: An attack the issuer mostly declines.
transition_in.introduces: Why those declines are still the merchant's problem.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Card testing therefore has to be stopped before authorization, in two layers: limits the merchant puts in front of any endpoint that can start a payment, and the provider's pre-authorization blocking, whose published results are vendor claims without baselines. Stripe's claim comes from the May 2025 post in which it announced a payments foundation model it says it uses against card testing.

evidence.what: Stripe: "simple firewall rules or filters based on a single heuristic such as IP addresses are usually not sufficient"; recommended merchant controls are CAPTCHA, requiring login before the payment form and rate limits; card-testing prevention is included in every Radar plan. Adyen: the bot-attack rule "detects and blocks transactions that come in at an unusually fast rate with suspicious payment properties ... This rule mostly prevents large scale attacks" and is in the basic tier with no configuration.
evidence.shows: Both providers supply a pre-authorization control by default and both say it is not enough on its own.
evidence.source: Stripe documentation, 'Card testing', https://docs.stripe.com/disputes/prevention/card-testing (n.d., accessed November 2026); Stripe documentation, 'How Radar works' (plans), https://docs.stripe.com/radar/how-radar-works (n.d., accessed November 2026); Adyen documentation, 'Machine learning rules', https://docs.adyen.com/risk-management/configure-your-risk-profile/machine-learning-rules (n.d., accessed November 2026)

evidence.what: Vendor claims: Stripe (May 2025), "While attacks are up industry-wide, they are down 80% on Stripe"; Adyen (October 2026), "increasing blocked card testing attacks by 28% on average, with zero impact on legitimate shoppers". Neither gives baseline, period or method.
evidence.shows: The figures are the vendors' own and cannot be compared.
evidence.source: Stripe blog, 'Using AI to optimize payments performance with the Payments Intelligence Suite', https://stripe.com/blog/using-ai-optimize-payments-performance-payments-intelligence-suite (15 May 2025); Jaap Stefels, 'Catching card testing at scale with real-time features', https://www.adyen.com/knowledge-hub/catching-card-testing-at-scale (4 October 2026)

transition_in.carries_over: Declines that cost the merchant.
transition_in.introduces: Where and how to stop the attempts earlier.

sections.heading: Risk Beyond the Payment: When the Merchant Is the Risk
sections.controlling_idea: The same structure, an estimate now and the facts later, applies to the business being paid: a provider that pays a merchant before the dispute window closes is exposed to that merchant, scores accounts and holds funds against the exposure, and publishes little about how.

advances_thesis.how: Extends the thesis from the payer to the payee and opens the thread that the compliance chapter picks up.

transition_in.carries_over: Card testing, where the merchant is the tool, and the fraud table's last row, a property of an account.
transition_in.introduces: Risk decided per account, about the party being paid.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Card testing makes the merchant the tool; merchant fraud and failure make it the subject, the account-level prediction problem of the fraud table: because a provider pays out before customers' right to dispute has expired it carries a credit exposure to every merchant, which both companies manage with account-level scores or funds held back.

evidence.what: Stripe, 2026: its risk decisions include "Is the business trustworthy? ... Has this business become suddenly popular, or is it under attack? Should we adjust a business' credit reserves?"; for platforms, an account risk score estimates the probability "that an account would cause losses to your platform".
evidence.shows: Stripe names account-level risk decisions and exposes one score to platforms.
evidence.source: Hangzhi Guo and others, 'Fine-tuning LLMs for risk assessment', https://stripe.dev/blog/training-llms-for-risk-assessment (9 October 2026); Stripe documentation, 'Account fraud prevention', https://docs.stripe.com/radar/account-fraud-prevention (n.d., accessed November 2026)

evidence.what: Adyen: "Adyen calculates the deposit requirement for your account daily, based on variables such as your processing volume and the number of chargebacks and refunds"; if exposure exceeds coverage "by more than EUR10,000, then Adyen automatically withholds funds from your next payout".
evidence.shows: Adyen documents a daily exposure calculation and an automatic hold.
evidence.source: Adyen documentation, 'Deposit', https://docs.adyen.com/account/balances/deposit (n.d., accessed November 2026)

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Stripe names the factors behind a reserve and both companies list the businesses they prohibit, but the credit criteria and models by which either accepts a merchant are not public, and for a platform the practical point is that a seller's loss the seller cannot cover falls on the platform or the provider, which is where the next chapters on compliance and platforms take over.

evidence.what: Stripe's support site names the factors behind a reserve ("industry conditions, payment activity, dispute rate, refund rate, and financial stability") with no formula or amounts; each company publishes a list of prohibited businesses; no credit criteria or models were found in documentation, help centers, sites or engineering posts (17 November 2026). Stripe: "responsibility for your connected accounts' negative balances can belong to your platform or to Stripe". Larkfield's terms: the studio carries a lost dispute; if its balance cannot cover it, the loss falls on Larkfield (ledger).
evidence.shows: Marks where the evidence stops and ties account risk to the platform's own liability.
evidence.source: Stripe documentation, 'Risk management with Connect', https://docs.stripe.com/connect/risk-management (n.d., accessed November 2026); _research/scenario-ledger.md

transition_in.carries_over: What the two companies document about account risk.
transition_in.introduces: What they do not, and what a platform should take from it.

sections.heading: Stripe and Adyen: Where They Differ
sections.controlling_idea: Stripe and Adyen document the same decision points and kinds of control, and a holdout that Adyen states and Stripe's documentation only implies, and differ in how fine a score they expose, how a rule's timing is chosen, how a change is tested and, most of all, in how much each has published about its models.

advances_thesis.how: Sets the documented facts of the earlier sections side by side and states what neither company has published.

flow.rationale: The table carries the facts in cells without retelling the earlier sections; the reading follows because it is advice drawn from the rows; the list of what is not public closes the section because it qualifies both columns. The section comes after merchant risk so that the gap in underwriting can be listed with the others.

transition_in.carries_over: Decision points, scores, holdouts, rules, card-testing controls and account risk described company by company.
transition_in.introduces: The same facts in one table, with the author's reading.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Seven aspects separate or align the two in the public record, from where a rule runs to what has been published about the model.

evidence.what: Where They Differ table, seven rows: decision before the network; exposed score and default block; holdout; testing a change; card-testing control; published model detail; published latency. Every Stripe and Adyen cell is a fact cited earlier in the chapter or 'Not public'; the last column is the author's inference.
evidence.shows: The required comparison; no cell introduces a fact the chapter has not already sourced.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: On Stripe an integrator should read the outcome of every payment and use the rule tester and traffic allocation; on Adyen it should decide for each rule whether it runs before or after authorization, check which tier its features need, and use control traffic and experiments to measure.

evidence.what: Follows from the table: Stripe exposes a finer score and per-rule rollout; Adyen exposes timing as a property of each rule and gates the fraud-risk model, custom rules and experiments behind premium features.
evidence.shows: Turns the differences into what to do on each provider.

transition_in.carries_over: The documented differences.
transition_in.introduces: What an integrator does differently on each.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Seven things were not found in either company's documentation, help center, site or engineering posts: the size and training data of Adyen's fraud-risk model, both companies' merchant underwriting (credit criteria and models, the amounts behind Stripe's reserve factors and Adyen's deposit calculation), the size of the Shield model now in production, how often Radar is retrained now, a latency figure for Adyen's whole risk decision, behavior on timeout at either, and how Stripe's payments foundation model relates to the model its engineers describe.

evidence.what: List of gaps, each checked against the sources read on 17 November 2026: Adyen's fraud-risk model beyond its family and weekly retraining (size, training data); merchant credit criteria and models at both, and the amounts behind Stripe's named reserve factors and behind Adyen's documented deposit calculation (its deposit page gives the exposure and coverage components); the size of the Shield model in production; Radar's current retraining interval (daily in 2019; "regular retraining" only in 2026); a latency figure for Adyen's whole risk decision; timeout behavior at both; the relation between the payments foundation model announced on 15 May 2025 and Shield (the October 2026 engineering post does not mention it).
evidence.shows: Keeps the reader from reading the table's blanks as differences in practice.
evidence.source: Ryan Drapeau and Sai Samant, 'Scaling Radar: Fighting fraud with agent-assisted machine learning', https://stripe.dev/blog/scaling-radar-fighting-fraud-with-agent-assisted-machine-learning (19 October 2026); Stripe blog, 'Using AI to optimize payments performance with the Payments Intelligence Suite', https://stripe.com/blog/using-ai-optimize-payments-performance-payments-intelligence-suite (15 May 2025); Adyen documentation, 'Risk management', https://docs.adyen.com/risk-management (n.d., accessed November 2026)

transition_in.carries_over: What the public record supports.
transition_in.introduces: Where it stops.

sections.heading: In Practice at Larkfield: Closing the Open Till and Pricing Two Thresholds
sections.controlling_idea: Larkfield's answer to the weekend was limits in front of the widget, not a stricter fraud model, and when it did set thresholds it priced them per product and refused to judge a new rule before its labels had arrived.

advances_thesis.how: Applies the card-testing controls and the break-even rule with ledger numbers, and replays the acceptance probe's mistake inside the fictional company.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: After the weekend Larkfield put three limits in front of the public booking widget (a challenge for guests who pay without logging in, a rate limit per studio in the payment service, and an alert on a studio's declined and blocked attempts) and left the providers' pre-authorization blocking on. paragraphs.controlling_idea: Pricing the threshold with the break-even rule gives two different answers for one studio: since a fraud case takes the payment back but the seat cost almost nothing, a first €49 membership payment should be blocked only above about a 96% chance of fraud and a €16 guest drop-in above about 52%; because neither provider maps its scale to a chance, these set the direction per product, not a dial position.

evidence.what: Ledger prices: membership €49.00 a month, drop-in €16.00, illustrative dispute fee €15.00. Assumptions, labeled: a member stays eight months on average (€392 of revenue); a class seat has no marginal cost, so a fraud case costs the studio the €15.00 fee. Membership: 392 ÷ (392 + 15) = 96%. Drop-in: 16 ÷ (16 + 15) = 52%.
evidence.shows: The same model and the same studio need two thresholds because the cost of a refused customer is more than twenty times higher for the membership.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md

sections.heading: When It Goes Wrong
sections.controlling_idea: A risk system fails quietly in three ways: the evaluation does not run, a rule or list switches the model off for some traffic, or good customers are refused without any error appearing; each needs its own detector.

advances_thesis.how: Shows the failure side of the synchronous estimate and of the merchant-set price.

flow.rationale: From the failure that is rarest and documented, through the one a merchant causes itself, to the one that is commonest and hardest to see, which is why it comes last and gets the detector the whole chapter has been building toward.

transition_in.carries_over: A risk setup that works as designed.
transition_in.introduces: The ways it fails without announcing it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A working risk setup can still fail quietly in three ways; the rarest is documented: when the risk evaluation itself fails, Stripe documents that the payment goes ahead marked as unknown risk, so a merchant should count and review those payments instead of treating the absence of a block as a pass.

evidence.what: Stripe: "In unusual cases, an error might cause risk evaluation to fail. If this happens, Stripe reports the payment as having unknown risk"; the example outcome has `"reason": "unknown_risk_level"` and `"type": "authorized"`. Adyen documents no equivalent.
evidence.shows: A documented state the merchant can monitor on one provider and a gap on the other.
evidence.source: Stripe documentation, 'Risk evaluation', https://docs.stripe.com/radar/risk-evaluation (n.d., accessed November 2026)

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A broad allow rule or a stale allow-list entry turns the model off for whatever it matches, and a rule that treats a retry differently from the first attempt gives the same customer two answers.

evidence.what: Stripe: allow rules "override the Stripe default rules"; "Allowlists can allow fraudsters to operate without restrictions and bypass controls", and entries on default fingerprint allow lists "have a maximum lifespan of 30 days"; retries are pinned to one allocation bucket. Adyen: allow rules have the highest priority.
evidence.shows: Both vendors warn about the failure and Stripe has built two guards against it.
evidence.source: Stripe documentation, 'Rules', https://docs.stripe.com/radar/rules (n.d., accessed November 2026); https://docs.stripe.com/radar/lists (n.d., accessed November 2026); Adyen documentation, 'Configure your risk profile', https://docs.adyen.com/risk-management/configure-your-risk-profile (n.d., accessed November 2026)

transition_in.carries_over: A failure of the provider's evaluation.
transition_in.introduces: A failure the merchant configures itself.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The commonest failure raises no error at all: a threshold or rule that refuses good customers shows up only as sales that did not happen, and the opposite mistake shows up months later as a dispute rate that crosses a card network's monitoring threshold.

evidence.what: Visa's Acquirer Monitoring Program (fact sheet, 2025) counts fraud reports and disputes against settled transactions and lowered its 'Excessive' merchant threshold in the EU, the US, Canada and Asia-Pacific to 150 basis points on 1 April 2026.
evidence.shows: The cost of too loose a threshold is enforced by the network, with a published number.
evidence.source: Visa, 'Visa Acquirer Monitoring Program Overview' fact sheet, https://corporate.visa.com/content/dam/VCOM/corporate/visa-perspectives/security-and-trust/documents/visa-acquirer-monitoring-program-fact-sheet-2025.pdf (2025)

evidence.what: Detection for the first mistake is a holdout or control group and the blocked-payment count per rule; for the second, the dispute rate by cohort month, read only after sixty days. The author's recommendation.
evidence.shows: Names the detector for each direction of error.

transition_in.introduces: The failure that leaves none.

conclusion.heading: What to Take Away
conclusion.synthesis: The decision point, the label delay, the threshold and card testing are one fact seen four ways: every risk decision is made before its evidence exists. The score is a forecast of a dispute; the model's quality is known two months late and only for what was allowed; the threshold is a bet placed with the merchant's money; and card testing is the case where the evidence never comes as a label at all. That is why the provider's part (the estimate) and the merchant's part (the price, the limits, the patience to wait for labels) cannot be swapped or merged.
conclusion.so_what: A team that believes the provider detects fraud will switch the product on, tighten it after an incident and call the result a success two weeks later. A team that sees an estimate and a price will set the threshold from its margins, keep a holdout, date every verdict sixty days out, and put a limit in front of every endpoint that can start a payment.

callback.to: The opening €1 payment at 03:14 on a Saturday, which nobody in the payment path could know was fraud.
callback.how: The reader can now say what could be known at that moment (a score, the shape of the traffic around it), what could not (the cardholder's consent), and that for this payment the useful control was a limit on the endpoint, not a better guess.

takeaway.content: Price your block threshold from the cost of a refused customer and the cost of a fraud case, per product; judge no model or rule change before sixty days of labels; keep a holdout; and limit every endpoint that can start a payment.
